title: CLO 2024.1 - Texture Scaling Feature
description: Updated to CLO 2024.1, with a comprehensive upgrade to the design experience! Explore in detail with CLO technical experts: texture scaling can now be adjusted using percentages or units, and overlapping scaling can be applied based on internal lines and textures.
transcript:
Hello everyone, in version 2024.1, we optimized the sticker code function, allowing you to enter the code directly using the hundred-point pen or unit number.  
Let's learn how to enter the code through this video.  
First, we need to ensure that the size is changed to the base code in the object window.  
In this file, I will use the middle code M as the base code.  
Use the editor code tool to select the heavy sticker.  
You can see that there is an extra size section in the property editor.  
From the menu on the right side, you can choose to use the unit number or hundred-point pen to enter the code.  
Using the unit number, you can enter the exact size of each sticker.  
Using the hundred-point pen, you can enter the hundred-point number of each sticker.  
Because in the industry, when users enter the code for stickers, they usually use the hundred-point pen instead of numbers.  
This is more appropriate for users’ habits when entering the code for stickers.  
So here we are.  
Use the hundred-point pen to modify the hundred-point number of the S code and the L code.  
You need to pay attention:  
Since the base code is M at this time, the number for M cannot be edited now.  
At this point, if we want to overlap the position of the sticker for the code, we can do so.  
You can select the point that needs to be overlapped.  
Right-click to select the coordinates that need to be overlapped.  
Select X and Y overlap here.  
Switch the code number to check the effect.  
Then, there is another situation:  
How to use the existing code information to enter the code.  
This will also be explained in this video.  
You can see that there is already a sticker on this board.  
The code information is marked with a curve.  
At this time, the code only involves a change of location.  
The size of the sticker does not change.  
First, move the sticker to one side.  
Then we only need to use the loop outline tool.  
Hook this curve.  
Then use the edit code tool.  
Copy the code of a certain point in this internal shape.  
Then select the sticker to paste.  
Then move the sticker back to the original position.  
Finally, look at the sticker code information on this board.  
You can see that the code of this sticker will have a position and size change.  
First, move the sticker to the side.  
Then hook this shape.  
Then we need to switch the tool to edit curve code.  
Copy the four points on this internal shape once.  
Then paste to the four points of the sticker.  
Then move the sticker back to the original position.  
The above is all the content regarding the sticker code in the shell.  
After using the new function,  
everyone will directly put the code in the shell,  
which will become more convenient.

chunks.content: # CLO 2024.1 - Texture Scaling Feature: Sticker Code Function This document explains the updated sticker code functionality in CLO 2024.1, focusing on entering and editing sticker codes using unit numbers and hundred-point pens, overlapping sticker positions, and reusing existing code data for precise control over sticker size and placement. ## Sticker Code Entry Methods: Unit Number vs. Hundred-Point Pen This section describes how to input sticker codes using either unit numbers or hundred-point pens, highlighting their differences and industry preferences. In CLO 2024.1, the sticker code function has been optimized to allow direct entry of codes via the hundred-point pen or unit number in the object window. To begin, set the base code size for your object—commonly the middle code "M" is used as the base. - **Unit Number Input:** Allows entering the exact size value of each sticker directly. - **Hundred-Point Pen Input:** Inputs the code as a hundred-point number, which aligns better with industry practices, as users typically use hundred-point pens rather than raw numbers when entering sticker codes. When the base code is set (e.g., "M"), its value is fixed and cannot be edited to maintain consistency. The hundred-point pen method is preferred for modifying sizes of other codes like "S" (small) and "L" (large). ## Overlapping Sticker Positions Using Coordinates This section covers how to overlap stickers by adjusting coordinate points for precise positioning. If you want to overlap the position of a sticker on the texture, you can do so by: 1. Selecting the point on the sticker that needs to be overlapped. 2. Right-clicking to access coordinate options. 3. Choosing to overlap on both the X and Y axes. Switching between code numbers allows you to verify the visual effect of the overlap. This method facilitates accurate alignment of sticker textures where multiple codes may coexist. ## Using Existing Code Information to Modify Stickers This section explains how to reuse and transfer existing sticker code information—such as position and size—from one sticker to another using curve and code editing tools. For stickers that already have code information, typically marked by curves on the texture board, you can adjust their placement without changing their size by: 1. Moving the sticker aside. 2. Using the loop outline tool to select (hook) the curve that contains the code information. 3. Using the edit code tool to copy the code from specific points on the internal shape. 4. Selecting the target sticker and pasting the copied code points. 5. Moving the sticker back to its original position. This process ensures that the pasted sticker inherits the exact position and size modifications from the source curve, maintaining visual consistency. Multiple points can be copied at once (e.g., four points) for complex shapes, allowing precise duplication of code information across stickers. ## Summary The CLO 2024.1 sticker code feature enhances usability by supporting direct code entry using hundred-point pens or unit numbers, aligning with industry standards.
